decks.title: Security in the Contemporary World — Part 1: Traditional and Non-traditional Security
goals: Explain what security means and why the term is kept for grave threats
Explain deterrence, defence, balance of power and alliance building, and internal security
Distinguish disarmament, arms control and confidence building
Explain human security (narrow and broad) and global security

slides.heading: Security in the Contemporary World
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what **security** means, the **traditional** view, and the **non-traditional** view.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what security means, traditional external and internal security, cooperation among rivals, human security and global security
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: What makes you feel safe? A strong army at the border, or clean water, a doctor nearby and a steady job? Both answers are part of how the world thinks about security today. In this part we first study the older, traditional view, which is about protecting the state from war. Then we see how a newer view puts people and the whole planet at the centre.

slides.heading: What does security mean?
slides.body_md: Security is **freedom from threats** to the **core values** of a country or people. Only **grave** threats count.

rows: From threats to core values: survival, territory, a way of life
Only grave ones that could seriously harm those values
Traditional view: the state. Newer views: people and the planet

visual.alt: Table: security means freedom from threats to core values; only grave threats count; the traditional view protects the state while newer views protect people and the planet

slides.narration: At its simplest, security means freedom from threats. But not every problem is a security problem. Scholars keep the word for dangers that could seriously harm the core values of a country or people, such as survival, territory and a way of life. If we called everything a security issue, the word would stop being useful. Notice the last row: the big debate is about whose security we mean.

slides.heading: The traditional view: a threat of war
slides.body_md: In the traditional view the **state** is protected, and the gravest threat is **military attack**.

visual.caption: Three choices in the traditional view

slides.narration: The traditional view starts with the state. Its biggest fear is an attack by another country, because that threatens territory, independence and the lives of citizens. Faced with such a threat, a government has three basic choices. It can give in. It can try to stop the attack from ever happening by making it too costly. Or it can fight to limit or end a war that has already begun.

slides.heading: Quick check: why keep the word narrow?
slides.body_md: Why do scholars use "security" only for very grave threats?
slides.narration: Think about what would happen to the idea of security if every everyday problem were included in it.

slides.heading: Four components of external security

rows: Make an attack too costly to try
Stop a rival from becoming far stronger

visual.alt: Table of the four components of traditional external security: deterrence before a war, defence during a war, balance of power all the time, alliance building before and during a war

slides.narration: Traditional external security rests on four ideas. Deterrence tries to prevent a war. Defence limits or ends a war once it starts. Balance of power means keeping watch on how strong rivals are, and building up when a neighbour grows much stronger. Alliance building means joining hands with other states. Alliances follow national interest, so they can change when interests change.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: name the component
slides.body_md: Read each action of an imagined country and name the component it shows.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask: has the war **already begun**? If yes, it is defence.
Step 2 — Is the aim to **stop an attack happening**? Deterrence.
Step 3 — Is it a reaction to a rival's **growing strength**? Balance of power.
Step 4 — Does it involve **other states** joining in? Alliance building.

rows: Warns that any attack will meet a crushing response
Aims to stop the attack happening
Sends troops to push back raiders across the border
Raises defence spending when a neighbour grows stronger
Signs a mutual-defence pact with two states

visual.alt: Worked example table: a warning of a crushing response is deterrence; pushing back raiders is defence; raising spending when a neighbour grows is balance of power; a mutual-defence pact is alliance building
visual.caption: Look for the clue word before naming the component.

slides.narration: Case questions often describe what a government does and ask you to name the idea. Use the clue in each action. A warning of a crushing response is about preventing war, so it is deterrence. Pushing back raiders means fighting has started, so it is defence. Spending more because a neighbour is growing is balance of power. A pact with two states is an alliance.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the components
slides.body_md: Match each component with what an imagined government does.
slides.narration: Use the same clues as in the worked example: timing, aim and partners.

slides.heading: Internal security
slides.body_md: Traditional security also covers **internal** order. After 1945 this mattered very differently in different parts of the world.

headers: Many new states of Asia and Africa
rows: External threats, especially in the Cold War
Both neighbours and internal separatist movements

visual.alt: Comparison table: after 1945 most Western powers worried mainly about external threats and were internally stable, while many new states of Asia and Africa faced both neighbours and internal separatist movements

slides.narration: Traditional security is not only about the border. After the Second World War, most Western powers were internally stable, so their main worry was external, especially during the Cold War. Many countries that became free in Asia and Africa faced a double challenge: disputes with neighbours and movements inside their borders that wanted separate states. For them, external and internal security were tied together.

slides.heading: Limits on violence
slides.body_md: Even in war, the traditional view accepts **limits**: spare **civilians** and surrendering soldiers, use force **in proportion** and only as a **last resort**.
slides.narration: The traditional view does not say anything goes. An old tradition of thought holds that force should be a last resort, should be used only in proportion to the threat, and should spare people who are not fighting, such as civilians and soldiers who have surrendered. These ideas lie behind many rules of war that countries have accepted.

slides.heading: Cooperation among rivals
slides.body_md: States that distrust each other can still **cooperate** to make war less likely.

rows: Gives up a whole category of weapons
Two rivals destroy all stocks of a nerve gas
Each side keeps at most fifty launchers

visual.alt: Table of three forms of cooperation within traditional security: disarmament gives up a weapon category, arms control caps or regulates weapons, confidence building shares information to avoid mistakes

slides.narration: Rivals can still cooperate. In disarmament they give up a whole kind of weapon. In arms control they keep weapons but accept limits on how many or what kind. In confidence building they share information, for example about army exercises, so that neither side mistakes a routine move for an attack. All three reduce the chance of war.

slides.narration: Here are some landmark agreements. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty came in 1968. In 1972 came the Biological Weapons Convention and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty between the United States and the Soviet Union. The Chemical Weapons Convention followed in 1992. Learn these four years carefully; they are often asked.

slides.heading: Quick check: the 1972 missile treaty
slides.body_md: The Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty of 1972 is an example of what?
slides.narration: Ask yourself: did the treaty abolish weapons, or did it limit them?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: abolish or regulate?
slides.body_md: Classify four agreements as **disarmament** or **arms control**.
bullets: Step 1 — Does the agreement **ban a whole category** of weapon? Then it is disarmament.
Step 2 — Does it **limit, cap or decide who may hold** weapons? Then it is arms control.
Step 3 — Write the classification **and** the reason.

rows: Abolishes making and holding biological weapons
Decides who may hold nuclear weapons

visual.alt: Worked example table: the Biological and Chemical Weapons Conventions abolish weapons and are disarmament; the ABM Treaty and the NPT regulate weapons and are arms control

slides.narration: Let us classify four agreements. The biological and chemical weapons conventions ban whole categories of weapons, so they are disarmament. The missile treaty only limited defence systems, and the non-proliferation treaty decided which countries could keep nuclear weapons, so both are arms control. India has not signed the non-proliferation treaty, which it sees as unequal.

slides.heading: Non-traditional security: whose security?
slides.body_md: The non-traditional view widens **whose** security matters and **which** threats count.
columns:
**Traditional**

- Protects the state
- Military threats
- Armed force and alliances

**Non-traditional**

- Protects people and humanity
- Also hunger, disease, climate
- Cooperation and development

rows: People and humanity as a whole
Also violence by states on people, hunger, disease, climate

visual.alt: Comparison of traditional and non-traditional security: whose security, the main threats and the main tools

slides.narration: The non-traditional view asks a different question: whose security? It looks beyond the state to individual human beings and to humanity as a whole. So the list of threats grows to include violence by a government against its own people, hunger, disease and climate change. The tools also change, from armies and alliances to cooperation, development and rights.

slides.heading: Human security: narrow and broad

visual.caption: Both views protect individuals; they differ on which threats count

slides.narration: Human security puts the individual at the centre. Everyone in this debate agrees that people must be protected. They differ on which threats to include. The narrow view focuses on violence, including violence by a person's own government. The broad view adds freedom from want: hunger, disease and natural disasters. One reason for this idea is that some governments have harmed their own citizens.

slides.heading: Global security

nodes.label: No single state can solve it

visual.alt: Flow: threats such as global warming, epidemics and terrorism cross borders, no single state can solve them, so countries must cooperate; this is global security
visual.caption: Why global security is a separate idea

slides.narration: Global security deals with threats that cross borders, such as global warming, epidemics and international terrorism. No country, however strong, can solve these alone. A rising sea does not stop at a border, and a virus travels on aeroplanes. So countries have to work together, and that cooperation is what global security is about.

slides.heading: Quick check: the narrow view
slides.body_md: The narrow concept of human security protects people mainly from what?
slides.narration: Remember the difference: the narrow view has one main threat, the broad view adds several more.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Freedom from grave threats to core values
Deterrence, defence, balance of power, alliances
A major concern for many new post-colonial states
Protect people: narrow (violence) or broad (also want)

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning of security, traditional external and internal security, cooperation among rivals, human security and global security

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Security means freedom from grave threats to core values. The traditional view protects the state through deterrence, defence, balance of power and alliances, and also worries about internal order. Rivals can still cooperate through disarmament, arms control and confidence building. The newer view protects people, narrowly from violence or broadly from want as well, and tackles global threats together.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Deterrence **before** war; defence **after** it begins. Do not swap them.
Disarmament **abolishes** a weapon type; arms control **regulates** it. NPT and ABM are arms control.
Learn the years: NPT 1968; BWC and ABM 1972; CWC 1992.
Narrow and broad human security agree on **protecting individuals**; they differ on **which threats**.
In source questions, **quote** the line, **name** the concept, **explain** it in one sentence.
slides.narration: A few exam tips. Keep deterrence and defence apart by timing. Remember that arms control regulates weapons while disarmament abolishes them. Learn the four treaty years. When you compare the two views of human security, say what they agree on as well as how they differ. And in source questions, quote, name and explain.

decks.title: Security in the Contemporary World — Part 2: New Threats, Cooperation and India
goals: Analyse terrorism, human rights, global poverty, migration and epidemics as threats
Distinguish refugees from internally displaced persons
Explain cooperative security, its levels and actors
Describe the four components of India's security strategy

slides.heading: New sources of threat, cooperation and India
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **new threats**, **cooperative security** and **India's strategy**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: terrorism, human rights, global poverty, migration, epidemics, cooperative security and India's strategy
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we look at threats that armies alone cannot defeat: terrorism, abuse of human rights, global poverty, forced migration and epidemics. Then we see how countries and other groups cooperate to deal with them, and finally how India puts together its own security strategy.

slides.heading: Why call these threats new?

visual.alt: Table contrasting the older focus on enemy armies, border wars and military balance with newer threats: attacks on civilians, rights abuses, poverty, migration and epidemics

slides.narration: Wars between armies have not disappeared, but other dangers now affect many more people. These newer threats often come from groups rather than states, travel across borders, and harm ordinary people directly. That is why they sit at the centre of the non-traditional view of security.

slides.heading: Terrorism
slides.body_md: **Terrorism** is political violence that deliberately and indiscriminately targets **civilians** to create fear.

visual.alt: Flow showing how terrorism works: violence against civilians spreads fear, which puts pressure on governments to serve the group's political aim
visual.caption: How terrorism uses fear

slides.narration: Terrorism means political violence aimed on purpose at ordinary people. Attacks on markets, trains or offices are meant to spread fear, and that fear is used to put pressure on governments to change a political situation. Because many groups work across borders, countries need to share information and act together against them.

slides.heading: Human rights as security
slides.body_md: Human rights are grouped into **three** broad categories.

rows: Freedom to speak, meet and vote
Clean water, health care, fair wages, schooling
Rights of colonised peoples and minorities
Self-rule; protection of indigenous and ethnic groups

visual.alt: Table of the three categories of human rights with examples: political rights, economic and social rights, and rights of colonised peoples and minorities

slides.narration: Human rights are now seen as part of security. They are usually grouped into three categories. Political rights include free speech and the vote. Economic and social rights include work, wages, health and schooling. The third category covers the rights of colonised peoples and of ethnic and indigenous minorities.

slides.heading: The debate on humanitarian intervention
slides.body_md: Should outside powers step in when a government seriously abuses its own people?
columns:
**For**

- Grave abuse cannot be ignored
- Collective action can save lives

**Concerns**

- Sovereignty is overridden
- Selective use by powerful states

rows: Grave abuse of people cannot be ignored
It can override a country's sovereignty
Powerful states may act selectively, for their own interests
Collective action can stop mass violence
It may worsen violence if badly planned

visual.alt: Two-sided table of the humanitarian intervention debate: arguments for (grave abuse, lives over borders, collective action) and concerns (sovereignty, selective use by powerful states, worsening violence)

slides.narration: A hard question follows. If a government badly abuses its people, should others intervene? Supporters say lives matter more than borders. Critics worry that powerful countries choose when to act according to their own interests, and that intervention can make violence worse. Most people agree it should be a last resort, decided collectively. In exams, present both sides calmly.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the threat
slides.body_md: Match each imagined news report with the threat it describes.
slides.narration: For each report, ask who is harmed and how: is it violence, denial of rights, disease or forced movement?

slides.heading: Global poverty

visual.alt: Flow: poverty and inequality cause hunger and weak health systems, which feed conflict and migration, whose effects cross borders
visual.caption: Why poverty is a security issue

slides.narration: Poverty is not only an economic problem. Large gaps between rich and poor regions, and fast population growth in some of the poorest countries, can lead to hunger, weak health systems and conflict. These push people to migrate and allow diseases to spread, so the effects reach far beyond the poor region itself.

slides.narration: Wars, persecution and disasters force people from their homes. If they cross an international border, they are refugees. If they stay inside their own country, they are internally displaced persons. Both groups face hunger, illness and loss of legal protection, and the places that receive them can come under great strain.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a source
slides.body_md: An imagined camp diary mentions people arriving from **across a river** after fighting, others from a **flooded district of the same country**, a feared **fever outbreak** and **rising market prices**.

rows: Underline who moves and whether a border is crossed
Mark each threat in the text: fighting, disease, prices

sections.heading: 1. Meaning of security and the traditional view
sections.body_md:
**Security** = freedom from threats to **core values** (survival, territory, way of life). Only **grave** threats, which could seriously damage those values, are treated as security issues; otherwise the idea becomes too wide.

**Traditional view:** the **state** is the object of security and the gravest danger is **military attack**, which threatens sovereignty, territory and civilian lives. A government facing war can surrender, deter or defend.

**Four components of external security:**
- **Deterrence:** prevent war by making it too costly for an attacker.
- **Defence:** limit or end a war once it begins.
- **Balance of power:** keep a check on the relative strength of rivals; build up when a neighbour grows much stronger.
- **Alliance building:** coalitions of states to deter or fight; based on national interest, so they shift over time.

**Why self-help:** there is no world government above states, so each relies on its own strength and partners.

key_terms.definition_md: Preventing an attack by making clear it would cost the attacker too much.
Keeping the strength of rivals from tilting sharply against one's own country.
A coalition of states formed to deter or meet military attack, guided by national interest.

sections.heading: 2. Internal security, limits on war and cooperation
sections.body_md:
**Internal security:** after 1945 most Western powers were stable at home and focused on external, Cold War threats. Many newly independent states of Asia and Africa faced **both** neighbours and separatist movements inside their borders.

**Limits on war:** force as a last resort, in proportion to the threat, sparing non-combatants and surrendering soldiers.

**Cooperation within traditional security:**
- **Disarmament:** giving up whole categories of weapons, e.g. the **Biological Weapons Convention (1972)** and the **Chemical Weapons Convention (1992)**.
- **Arms control:** regulating weapons, e.g. the **Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (1972)** between the USA and the USSR, and the **Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968)**, under which states that tested before 1967 kept their weapons and others gave up the option. India has not signed the NPT and calls it discriminatory.
- **Confidence building:** sharing military information (exercises, deployments) to avoid surprise and mistaken war.

key_terms.definition_md: Agreement to give up or destroy a whole kind of weapon.
Agreement to limit or regulate weapons without abolishing them.
Exchange of military information between rivals to prevent misunderstanding.

sections.heading: 3. Non-traditional security: human and global
sections.body_md:
**Non-traditional security** widens **whose** security counts (people, humanity) and **which** threats count (beyond the military).

**Human security** protects **individuals**. One reason for the idea: in many cases governments have harmed their own citizens.
- **Narrow concept:** protection mainly from **violence**.
- **Broad concept:** also **freedom from want**: hunger, disease, natural disasters.
Both camps agree people come first; they differ on the list of threats.

**Global security:** threats such as **global warming, international terrorism and epidemics** that cross borders and that no country can tackle alone.

key_terms.definition_md: Security of individual people rather than of the state alone.
Security against threats that affect the whole world and need joint action.

sections.heading: 4. New threats: terrorism, human rights and poverty
sections.body_md:
**Terrorism:** political violence deliberately aimed at **civilians** to create fear and force political change; often by **non-state** groups working across borders.

**Human rights:** three categories: **political**; **economic and social**; **rights of colonised peoples and ethnic and indigenous minorities**. The debate on **humanitarian intervention** weighs protecting people against **sovereignty** and the risk of **selective** action by powerful states.

**Global poverty:** the gap between rich and poor regions and rapid population growth in some poor countries feed hunger, conflict and migration, with effects across borders.

key_terms.definition_md: Political violence that targets civilians on purpose to spread fear.
Action by outside powers inside a country to stop grave abuse of its people.

sections.heading: 5. Migration and health epidemics
sections.body_md:
**Refugees** flee war, persecution or disaster **across an international border**. **Internally displaced persons** are uprooted but **stay inside** their country. Both face hunger, illness and lack of protection; host areas face strain on services and prices.

**Epidemics** (HIV/AIDS, and later outbreaks and pandemics) spread through **travel, trade and migration**, overload health systems and disrupt economies. Border closures alone are not enough; shared data, research and health aid are needed.

sections.heading: 6. Cooperative security and India's security strategy
sections.body_md:
**Cooperative security:** joint action against non-traditional threats at **bilateral, regional, continental or global** levels, involving states, **international organisations**, **NGOs**, businesses and prominent individuals. **Force** may be used only as a **last resort**, preferably with collective approval (e.g. against terrorists or mass abuse).

**India's security strategy (four components):**
1. **Military capabilities:** conflicts with neighbours and a nuclear-armed neighbourhood; nuclear tests in **1974** and **1998**; a stated policy of **credible minimum deterrence** and **no first use**.
2. **International norms and institutions:** universal, non-discriminatory disarmament, decolonisation, a fairer world order, the **UN** system.
3. **Internal security challenges:** handled through **democratic** and constitutional means, such as dialogue and protection of minority rights.
4. **Economic development:** reducing poverty, inequality and deprivation.

key_terms.definition_md: Security achieved through joint action of many states and other actors, with force as a last resort.
A pledge not to be the first to use nuclear weapons in a conflict.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Swapping **deterrence** (before war) and **defence** (once war begins).
- Calling the NPT or ABM Treaty **disarmament**: they are **arms control**.
- Calling people who flee within their own country **refugees**: they are **internally displaced persons**.
- Listing only two categories of human rights.
- Giving personal opinions on current conflicts. Stick to concepts and agreed facts.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points, or a definition with an example (30–50 words).
- 3 marks: three distinct points (50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five headed points (80–120 words); evaluation questions need both sides and a conclusion.
- Source questions (4 marks): quote, name, explain; part (c) has an internal choice.

**Sources in SOYL practice** are imagined documents written for practice; your board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: In its most basic sense, what does "security" in world politics mean?

options.text_md: The total amount a country spends on its army in a year
Freedom from threats to the core values of a country or people
The number of allies a country has in a military pact
The ability of a country to export more than it imports

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Freedom from threats to the core values of a country or people. Security is about being free from threats to core values (survival, territory, a way of life). Defence spending, alliances and trade surpluses are means or unrelated measures, not the meaning itself.

questions.stem_md: Why do scholars limit the term "security" to very grave threats only?

options.text_md: Because small threats are always handled by the United Nations
Because only military threats can ever endanger a country
Because governments are not allowed to discuss minor problems
Because calling every problem a security issue would make the idea too wide to be useful

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Because calling every problem a security issue would make the idea too wide to be useful. If every difficulty (a traffic jam, a price rise) were a security issue, the concept would lose meaning. So it is kept for dangers that could seriously harm core values if not dealt with. The other options are false claims.

questions.stem_md: The imagined country Veloria announces that any attack on it will be met with a response so costly that the attacker will regret it. Which component of traditional security is Veloria relying on?

options.text_md: Deterrence
Defence
Balance of power
Alliance building

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Deterrence. Deterrence aims to **prevent** a war by making the cost of attacking too high. Defence is about limiting or ending a war once it has begun; balance of power and alliances are about the distribution of strength among states.

questions.stem_md: After its border posts are attacked, the imagined country Karvel moves troops to repel the attackers and push them back. This is an example of

options.text_md: deterrence
disarmament
defence
confidence building

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** defence. Defence means limiting or ending a war that has already started by defeating the attacking forces. Deterrence works before an attack; disarmament and confidence building are forms of cooperation, not fighting.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined neighbours, Arvania and Belmora, are roughly equal in strength. Arvania's economy and army suddenly start growing much faster. Under the traditional view, how is Belmora most likely to respond?

options.text_md: Disband its army because a stronger neighbour makes war impossible
Ignore the change, since power never affects security
Build up its own strength or seek partners so that the balance is not tilted against it
Ask Arvania to join its own military alliance immediately

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Build up its own strength or seek partners so that the balance is not tilted against it. States watch the **balance of power** closely: if a neighbour grows much stronger, the other tries to restore the balance by building its own capabilities or forming alliances. Disbanding or ignoring the change runs against this logic.

questions.stem_md: Alliances in traditional security are usually based on

options.text_md: national interests, so they can change when those interests change
permanent friendship that never changes
a common religion shared by all members
orders from the United Nations Security Council

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** national interests, so they can change when those interests change. An alliance is a coalition of states formed to deter or defend against attack, and it rests on national interest. When interests shift, alliances shift too, so they are not permanent or based on faith or UN orders.

questions.stem_md: Many countries that became independent in Asia and Africa after 1945 faced a security challenge different from that of most Western European states. What was it?

options.text_md: They faced no external threats because the Cold War protected them
They faced only internal threats and never had border disputes
They were barred from building their own armies
They faced threats both from neighbours and from separatist movements inside their borders

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** They faced threats both from neighbours and from separatist movements inside their borders. Newly independent states often had border disputes with neighbours **and** internal movements seeking separate states, so external and internal security were linked. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md: Which idea from the tradition of limiting violence in war is part of traditional security thinking?

options.text_md: Any amount of force is acceptable once a war has started
Force should spare non-combatants and be used only in proportion to the threat
Prisoners of war have no protection at all
Wars should be fought only by private armies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Force should spare non-combatants and be used only in proportion to the threat. Traditional security also accepts limits on the use of force: protecting civilians and unarmed or surrendering soldiers, and using force proportionately and as a last resort.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the traditional view, the greatest danger to a country comes from military threats.

**Reason (R):** Military action by another country can endanger the territory, sovereignty and lives of ordinary people.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: military force threatens the core of sovereignty (territory, independence) and also the lives of civilians, which is why the traditional view ranks it highest.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After the Second World War, internal security was less of a concern for most Western powers.

**Reason (R):** All newly independent countries of Asia and Africa had no internal conflicts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: the stable Western democracies mostly had internal peace, so they focused on external threats. R is false: many new states faced separatist and internal conflicts.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the traditional view, a government facing a threat of war has three basic choices: to surrender, to prevent the attack by raising its cost, or to defend itself once war begins.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** These are the three classic options; deterrence covers the second and defence the third. Surrender is rarely chosen but remains a logical option.

questions.stem_md: Trying to prevent a rival country from becoming much stronger than one's own is called maintaining the ___ of power.
questions.solution_md: This is the balance of power: states try to keep the distribution of strength from tilting sharply against them.

questions.stem_md: Match each component of traditional external security with what an imagined government does under it.

options.text_md: Deterrence
Defence
Balance of power
Alliance building

match_right.text_md: Fights to drive back forces that have already crossed the border
Signs a mutual-defence pact with two like-minded countries
Warns that an attack will bring unacceptable losses to the attacker
Expands its own capabilities when a neighbour grows much stronger

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Deterrence prevents war; defence ends or limits it; balance of power watches relative strength; alliances pool strength through a coalition.

questions.stem_md: How does deterrence differ from defence in traditional security? Give one point for each.
questions.solution_md: One point on the timing and purpose of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Deterrence** works **before** a war: a country makes clear that an attacker would suffer unbearable costs, so the attack never happens.
2. **Defence** works **after** fighting begins: the country uses force to limit the damage, repel the attacker and end the war.

marking_scheme.step: Deterrence: preventing war by raising its cost
Defence: limiting or ending a war once started

questions.stem_md: Why are alliances in traditional security described as temporary? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: Link alliances to interests and show that changing interests change alliances.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Alliances are formed to serve **national interests**, such as deterring a common rival; when that rival weakens or interests diverge, the reason for the alliance disappears.
2. A former **opponent** may later become a partner, so countries **switch** sides as circumstances change.

marking_scheme.step: Interests and partners change over time

questions.stem_md: Traditional security is mainly about force, yet it also recognises cooperation. Explain three forms of such cooperation between states.
questions.solution_md: Name and explain disarmament, arms control and confidence building.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Disarmament:** states agree to give up certain kinds of weapons altogether, for example biological or chemical weapons.
2. **Arms control:** states accept limits on how weapons are acquired, developed or deployed, such as caps on missile defences.
3. **Confidence building:** rivals share information about military plans and exercises so that neither side misreads the other and goes to war by mistake.

questions.stem_md: Explain the four components of the traditional notion of external security. Why do states rely on these means?
questions.solution_md: Four components, each explained, and a closing point on why states depend on them.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Deterrence:** a state prevents war by convincing a rival that an attack would cost far more than it could gain.
2. **Defence:** if war comes, the state fights to limit damage and push the attacker back.
3. **Balance of power:** states keep a watch on relative strength and build their own capabilities when a rival grows much stronger.
4. **Alliance building:** states form coalitions to add to their combined strength; these follow national interest and can change.
5. **Why:** in the traditional view there is **no world government** to protect a country, so each state must rely on its own power and partners to safeguard its sovereignty.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: self-help in the absence of a world authority

questions.stem_md: Which international agreement of 1972 banned the production and possession of biological weapons?

options.text_md: The Biological Weapons Convention
The Chemical Weapons Convention
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
The Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Biological Weapons Convention. The Biological Weapons Convention dates from 1972. The Chemical Weapons Convention is from 1992, the NPT from 1968, and the ABM Treaty (1972) limited missile defence systems, not biological weapons.

questions.stem_md: The Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty of 1972 between the United States and the Soviet Union is an example of

options.text_md: complete disarmament
arms control
humanitarian intervention
cooperative security led by NGOs

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** arms control. The treaty did not abolish weapons; it **limited** missile defence systems so that neither side would feel safe enough to strike first. That is arms control, not disarmament.

questions.stem_md: Why is the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968) described as arms control rather than disarmament?

options.text_md: It required every country in the world to destroy all its nuclear weapons at once
It banned only biological and chemical weapons
It allowed the countries that had tested nuclear weapons before 1967 to keep them, while others agreed not to acquire them
It was signed only by the United States and the Soviet Union

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It allowed the countries that had tested nuclear weapons before 1967 to keep them, while others agreed not to acquire them. The NPT regulated **who** could hold nuclear weapons: the states that had tested them before 1 January 1967 kept them and the rest gave up the option. It did not abolish them, so it is arms control.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** India has not signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

**Reason (R):** India has regarded the treaty as discriminatory because it divides countries into those allowed and those not allowed to hold nuclear weapons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R gives India's stated reason for staying out: it sees the treaty as unequal, favouring the countries that already had nuclear weapons.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these arms-control and disarmament agreements in the order in which they were concluded, earliest first.

options.text_md: Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
Chemical Weapons Convention
Biological Weapons Convention and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (a) → (c) → (b). NPT 1968, then the BWC and ABM Treaty in 1972, then the CWC in 1992.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: The ___ Weapons Convention of 1992 bans the making, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons.
questions.solution_md: The Chemical Weapons Convention (1992) is a disarmament agreement covering chemical weapons.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined rivals agree (i) to stop all production of a deadly nerve gas and destroy their stocks, and (ii) to cap the number of missile launchers each may keep. Classify each step and give a reason.
questions.solution_md: Abolishing a weapon type = disarmament; capping or regulating = arms control.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) is **disarmament**: a whole category of weapon is **given up** and destroyed.
(ii) is **arms control**: the weapons stay, but their **number is limited** by agreement so that the rivalry stays stable.

questions.stem_md: The armies of two imagined neighbours, Sorun and Teval, inform each other in advance before large exercises near their border. What is this practice called, and how does it help security?
questions.solution_md: Name the practice and link it to reducing mistrust.

answer.model_answer_md: It is **confidence building**. By sharing information in advance, each side knows the exercise is not preparation for an attack, so **misunderstanding and accidental war** become less likely and trust grows.

marking_scheme.step: Reduces misperception and the risk of war by mistake

questions.stem_md: Non-traditional notions of security differ from traditional ones mainly because they

options.text_md: deal only with threats from foreign armies
reject any role for international cooperation
apply only to the largest military powers
focus on the security of people and of humanity as a whole, not only of states

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** focus on the security of people and of humanity as a whole, not only of states. The non-traditional view widens the "referent" of security from the state to human beings and the whole planet, and widens threats beyond military ones.

questions.stem_md: Supporters of the **narrow** concept of human security focus mainly on protecting individuals from

options.text_md: all forms of want, including hunger and disease
loss of national prestige
trade deficits
violence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** violence. The narrow concept is about protecting people from violence, much of it by their own state or armed groups. The broad concept adds threats such as hunger, disease and disasters.

questions.stem_md: An imagined charter says that people must be free both from violence and from hunger, disease and the effects of disasters. Which idea of security does this charter reflect?

options.text_md: The narrow concept of human security
Traditional external security
The broad concept of human security
Balance of power

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The broad concept of human security. Covering hunger, disease and disasters along with violence ("freedom from want" as well as "freedom from fear") is the broad concept of human security.

questions.stem_md: Which of these threats is the best example of a **global security** concern?

options.text_md: A quarrel between two villages over a grazing field
A rise in sea level that endangers low-lying coastal countries everywhere
A dispute between two firms over a contract
A single country's decision to change its school syllabus

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A rise in sea level that endangers low-lying coastal countries everywhere. Global security deals with threats that no single state can solve and that affect people across borders, such as rising seas from global warming. The others are local or private matters.

questions.stem_md: A key reason scholars developed the idea of human security was the observation that

options.text_md: in many cases people have been killed or harmed by their own governments rather than by foreign armies
foreign invasions stopped completely after 1945
states no longer have armies to protect their people
only economic growth matters to ordinary citizens

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** in many cases people have been killed or harmed by their own governments rather than by foreign armies. A secure state does not always mean secure people: governments have sometimes turned violence against their own citizens. Human security puts people at the centre to address this.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Human security gives priority to the protection of people over the protection of states.

**Reason (R):** Global security threats such as global warming cannot be tackled by a single country acting alone.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R is about global security (threats needing international cooperation), not the reason human security centres on people. So R does not explain A.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Supporters of the narrow and the broad concepts of human security disagree about whether individuals, rather than states, should be protected.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Both camps agree that **individuals** are to be protected. They differ only on **which threats** count: violence alone (narrow) or also hunger, disease and disasters (broad).

questions.stem_md: State two differences between the traditional notion of security and human security.
questions.solution_md: Contrast the object protected and the range of threats.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Whose security:** traditional security protects the **state** (territory, sovereignty); human security protects **individual people**.
2. **Which threats:** traditional security looks mainly at **military** threats; human security also includes violence by one's own state, hunger, disease and disasters.

marking_scheme.step: Object of security: state vs people
Range of threats: military vs wider

questions.stem_md: Why is "global security" a separate idea from national security? Explain with two examples of global threats.
questions.solution_md: Define the idea (cross-border, needs cooperation) and give two explained examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
Global security covers dangers that **cross borders** and that **no single state can handle alone**, so cooperation among countries is needed.
1. **Global warming:** rising temperatures and sea levels affect many countries at once, whoever caused the emissions.
2. **Health epidemics:** a new infectious disease can travel through trade and travel to every continent within weeks.

questions.stem_md: Terrorism refers to political violence that

options.text_md: is used only by regular armies in declared wars
deliberately targets civilians, without discrimination, to create fear
is always approved by the United Nations
never crosses national borders

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** deliberately targets civilians, without discrimination, to create fear. Terrorism is political violence aimed deliberately and indiscriminately at civilians in order to spread fear and pressure governments. It is not conventional war and often crosses borders.

questions.stem_md: What is the usual aim of a terrorist group that attacks crowded public places?

options.text_md: To capture and govern the territory where the attack took place
To win a declared war against another country's army
To earn money from the people who are attacked
To use the fear created among people to force a change in a political situation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To use the fear created among people to force a change in a political situation. Terrorists use violence against ordinary people to spread fear and so pressure governments or societies into political change. They usually cannot win a conventional war or govern territory directly.

questions.stem_md: People in the imagined country Mirvana demand clean water, health care and a minimum wage. Which category of human rights are they asking for?

options.text_md: Economic and social rights
Political rights
Rights of colonised peoples
Rights of states to self-defence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Economic and social rights. Water, health care and wages are economic and social rights. Political rights cover free speech and assembly; the third category concerns colonised peoples and indigenous minorities.

questions.stem_md: Why is "humanitarian intervention" by outside powers to stop rights abuses in another country a matter of debate?

options.text_md: Everyone agrees it should happen automatically whenever a government is criticised
International law forbids any discussion of human rights
Some argue it protects people, while others worry that powerful states may use it selectively to suit their own interests
It is only about trade and has nothing to do with rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Some argue it protects people, while others worry that powerful states may use it selectively to suit their own interests. One side holds that the world must act to protect people from grave abuse; the other points out that interventions can override sovereignty and that strong states choose when and where to act according to their own interests.

questions.stem_md: Fighting forces a family in the imagined country Tarvania to flee across the border into a neighbouring country. In world politics this family is described as

options.text_md: internally displaced persons
economic migrants
refugees
non-combatant soldiers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** refugees. People who flee war, persecution or disaster **across an international border** are refugees. If they had fled within Tarvania's own borders, they would be internally displaced persons.

questions.stem_md: After floods and armed clashes, thousands of people in the imagined country Ondara leave their villages but stay inside Ondara, living in camps near the capital. They are

options.text_md: internally displaced persons
refugees
migrant workers abroad
stateless citizens of another country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** internally displaced persons. They have been forced from their homes but have **not crossed an international border**, so they are internally displaced persons, not refugees.

questions.stem_md: Why is global poverty treated as a source of insecurity in world politics?

options.text_md: Poor countries usually have the largest armies
Poverty affects only the people concerned and has no wider effect
Rich countries are always the cause of every war
Poverty in poorer regions is linked to conflict, migration and disease, which spill over borders

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Poverty in poorer regions is linked to conflict, migration and disease, which spill over borders. Widespread poverty and the gap between rich and poor regions feed conflicts, push people to migrate and weaken health systems, so the problems spread beyond any one country.

questions.stem_md: Why are health epidemics considered a threat to security and not only a medical problem?

options.text_md: Epidemics affect only the country where a disease first appears
Diseases spread across borders through travel, trade and migration, and can disrupt whole societies and economies
Only military hospitals can treat infectious diseases
Epidemics are always caused by deliberate attacks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Diseases spread across borders through travel, trade and migration, and can disrupt whole societies and economies. Infectious diseases move with people and goods; HIV/AIDS and later pandemics showed they can overload health systems, reduce working populations and disrupt economies far from where they began.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Global poverty can become a source of insecurity beyond the countries where it is found.

**Reason (R):** Poverty and inequality can contribute to conflict and to large movements of people across borders.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: through conflict and migration, poverty in one region affects neighbours and the wider world.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A country can always protect itself from an epidemic by closing its own borders, without cooperating with others.

**Reason (R):** Infectious diseases spread through travel, trade and the movement of people.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: closed borders are never complete and diseases are best contained through shared information, research and health support, so cooperation is needed. R is true.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Terrorism is a form of conventional war fought between the regular armies of two countries.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Terrorism is non-conventional political violence that deliberately targets civilians. It is usually carried out by groups, not by regular national armies facing each other in battle.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined news report with the new source of threat it describes.

options.text_md: A bomb is set off in a busy market to frighten the public
A government jails journalists who criticise it
A new virus spreads to twelve countries in a month
Fifty thousand people cross a border to escape fighting

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Indiscriminate violence on civilians = terrorism; silencing critics = denial of political rights; cross-border disease = epidemic; fleeing across a border = refugees.

questions.stem_md: People who flee their homes but remain within their own country's borders are called internally ___ persons.
questions.solution_md: They are internally displaced persons; they differ from refugees, who cross an international border.

questions.stem_md: Name the three broad categories into which human rights are commonly grouped in world politics, with one example of any two.
questions.solution_md: All three categories named, with two examples.

answer.model_answer_md: The three categories are **political rights**, **economic and social rights**, and the **rights of colonised peoples and of ethnic and indigenous minorities**. Examples: freedom of speech (political); the right to a fair wage or to health care (economic and social).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between refugees and internally displaced persons, with an imagined example of each.
questions.solution_md: The test is whether an international border is crossed.

answer.model_answer_md: **Refugees** flee war, persecution or disaster **across an international border**, e.g. villagers from an imagined Country A who escape into Country B. **Internally displaced persons** are forced from their homes but **stay within their own country**, e.g. flood victims who move to camps in their own state.

marking_scheme.step: Refugees: cross a border, with example
IDPs: remain inside the country, with example

questions.stem_md: Explain why terrorism is called a "new" source of threat even though political violence is old.
questions.solution_md: Three features that make it different from conventional threats.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Targets:** it deliberately and indiscriminately strikes **civilians** in markets, transport or offices rather than armies.
2. **Actors:** it is often carried out by **groups that are not states**, which are hard to deter with traditional military power.
3. **Reach:** many groups work **across borders** using modern communication, finance and travel, so no single country can deal with them alone.

questions.stem_md: How can large-scale migration become a security concern for both the people who move and the countries they move to? Give three points.
questions.solution_md: One point on migrants' own insecurity, one on pressures for hosts, one on interstate tension or the need for cooperation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **For migrants:** people fleeing conflict or disaster often lack food, shelter, health care and legal protection, so their own security is at risk.
2. **For host countries:** a sudden inflow can strain housing, jobs and public services, especially in poorer border regions.
3. **For relations between states:** disputes may arise over who should accept and support displaced people, which makes cooperation and international help important.

marking_scheme.step: Interstate tension or need for cooperation

questions.stem_md: Explain any five new sources of threat to security in the contemporary world.
questions.solution_md: Five distinct threats, each explained as a threat to people or states.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Terrorism:** groups deliberately attack civilians to spread fear and force political change, often operating across borders.
2. **Violation of human rights:** governments or armed groups may deny people political, economic or social rights, or attack their own citizens.
3. **Global poverty:** poverty and the gap between rich and poor regions feed conflict, hunger and instability.
4. **Migration and refugees:** wars and disasters drive people from their homes, within or across borders, straining both them and host areas.
5. **Health epidemics:** diseases such as HIV/AIDS and later pandemics travel quickly and can disrupt societies and economies worldwide.

questions.stem_md: Human rights are now seen as part of security. Explain the main categories of human rights and evaluate the debate over outside intervention to protect them.
questions.solution_md: Three categories, then both sides of the intervention debate and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Political rights:** freedom of speech, assembly and the vote.
2. **Economic and social rights:** work, a fair wage, health care, education and food.
3. **Rights of colonised peoples and minorities:** self-determination and protection of indigenous and ethnic groups.
4. **For intervention:** supporters say the world cannot stand aside when a government commits grave abuses against its own people; human life matters more than borders.
5. **Against or with caution:** critics say intervention can violate sovereignty, may be used **selectively** by powerful states for their own interests, and can worsen violence; so most argue it should be a last resort, decided collectively.

marking_scheme.step: Rights of colonised peoples and minorities

questions.stem_md: Why do many non-traditional threats call for cooperative security rather than military force?

options.text_md: Threats such as epidemics, poverty and global warming cannot be defeated by armies and need joint action by many actors
Armies have been abolished in most countries
Cooperation is cheaper than any other policy in every case
International law forbids states from keeping armies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Threats such as epidemics, poverty and global warming cannot be defeated by armies and need joint action by many actors. You cannot fight a virus or rising sea levels with tanks; such threats need shared information, resources and policies among states, international bodies and others.

questions.stem_md: A medical charity, a group of neighbouring governments and a UN agency together run vaccination drives in an imagined region hit by an epidemic. This is an example of

options.text_md: traditional deterrence
cooperative security involving state and non-state actors
balance of power politics
unilateral military defence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** cooperative security involving state and non-state actors. Cooperative security can be bilateral, regional or global and may include international organisations and non-governmental groups, as here.

questions.stem_md: In cooperative security, what is the role of force?

options.text_md: It is the first and main tool for every threat
It can never be used under any circumstances
It may be used only as a last resort, ideally with collective approval, for example against terrorists or grave abuses
It can be used by any state whenever it wishes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It may be used only as a last resort, ideally with collective approval, for example against terrorists or grave abuses. Cooperation is the main approach, but force is not ruled out: it is a last resort, preferably legitimised collectively, such as to deal with terrorists or to stop mass abuse.

questions.stem_md: India conducted nuclear tests in which years?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1974 and 1998. India's nuclear tests were held at Pokhran in 1974 and in 1998.

questions.stem_md: An imagined government white paper says that lifting citizens out of poverty and reducing inequality is part of national security. Which component of India's security strategy does this match?

options.text_md: Strengthening military capabilities
Strengthening international norms and institutions
Building military alliances with great powers
Developing the economy so that people are not poor and deprived

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Developing the economy so that people are not poor and deprived. India's strategy includes economic development to remove poverty and inequality, on the view that a secure country needs secure, prosperous citizens.

questions.stem_md: India has supported universal and non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament and decolonisation, and has worked within the United Nations. Which component of its security strategy do these choices reflect?

options.text_md: Meeting internal security challenges
Strengthening military capabilities
Strengthening international norms and institutions
Economic development

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Strengthening international norms and institutions. Backing global rules (disarmament, decolonisation), UN processes and similar efforts strengthens international norms and institutions.

questions.stem_md: India describes its nuclear weapons policy as one of "credible minimum deterrence" with a commitment to

options.text_md: first use whenever threatened
no first use
complete secrecy about its doctrine
sharing weapons with allies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** no first use. India's stated doctrine is a minimum credible deterrent and no first use of nuclear weapons.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Strengthening military capabilities has been one component of India's security strategy.

**Reason (R):** India has been involved in conflicts with neighbours and is located in a region with nuclear-armed states.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: past conflicts and a difficult neighbourhood are reasons India gives for maintaining strong defence capabilities.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cooperative security involves only national governments; international organisations and voluntary groups have no role in it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Cooperative security includes international bodies (such as UN agencies), regional groupings, NGOs, businesses and even well-known individuals, not just governments.

questions.stem_md: At what levels can cooperative security operate? Give an imagined example of any one level.
questions.solution_md: Levels named, with one fitting example.

answer.model_answer_md: It can be **bilateral** (two countries), **regional**, **continental** or **global**. Example: five neighbouring imagined countries share flood warnings and send rescue teams to each other during the monsoon, which is **regional** cooperation.

questions.stem_md: How does India try to meet internal security challenges, according to its security strategy? Give two ways.
questions.solution_md: Two ways that use democratic and constitutional means.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It tries to deal with internal conflicts through **democratic** means: negotiation with groups that have grievances and giving them a voice.
2. It uses **constitutional** arrangements such as protecting minority rights and sharing power with regions, while keeping law and order.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three components of India's security strategy.
questions.solution_md: Any three of the four components, each with a brief explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Military capability:** India maintains armed forces and a nuclear deterrent because of past conflicts and its neighbourhood.
2. **International norms and institutions:** it backs disarmament, a just world order and the UN system.
3. **Development:** it treats economic growth and the removal of poverty and inequality as a basis of security.
(Also: meeting internal challenges democratically.)

questions.stem_md: An imagined student argues that "military power alone can keep a country secure today". Evaluate this view in three points.
questions.solution_md: A balanced evaluation: what military power can do, what it cannot, and the need for cooperation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Military power is still needed against **external attack**, so it is part of security.
2. But threats such as **epidemics, global warming, poverty and terrorism** cannot be defeated by armies alone.
3. These need **cooperation** among states, international bodies and citizens, and development at home, so the view is only partly correct.

questions.stem_md: Describe the four components of India's security strategy. Which of these addresses non-traditional threats most directly? Explain.
questions.solution_md: Four components and a reasoned choice of the one closest to non-traditional security.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Strengthening military capabilities:** India has faced conflicts with neighbours and lives in a nuclear-armed region; it tested nuclear devices in 1974 and 1998 and follows minimum deterrence.
2. **Strengthening international norms and institutions:** support for universal disarmament, decolonisation and the UN system.
3. **Meeting internal security challenges:** handling internal conflicts through democratic, constitutional means.
4. **Developing the economy:** reducing poverty, inequality and deprivation.
5. **Non-traditional threats:** economic development speaks most directly to **human security**, because it tackles hunger, disease and want that make people insecure.

questions.stem_md: "Non-traditional threats demand cooperative security." Evaluate this statement with examples.
questions.solution_md: Why cooperation is needed, who takes part, an example, the limited role of force, and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Nature of the threats:** global warming, epidemics, terrorism and refugee flows cross borders, so no single state can deal with them.
2. **Many actors:** cooperation may be bilateral, regional or global and can include international bodies, NGOs and businesses, each bringing resources and knowledge.
3. **Example:** controlling an epidemic needs shared data, vaccines and health workers across countries.
4. **Role of force:** force is not ruled out, but is a **last resort**, ideally approved collectively, for example against terrorists.
5. **Judgement:** the statement is largely valid, though states still keep militaries for traditional threats; the two approaches work side by side.

questions.stem_md: Read the source on the imagined defence review of Veloria and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Deterrence = preventing attack by raising its cost.

**(b)** A mutual-defence pact is an alliance.

**(c) (i)** Advance notice = confidence building; a cap = arms control.

**OR (c) (ii)** Any two sensible reasons linked to cost or stability.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** "We will keep **enough strength to make any attack too costly** to try."

**(b)** **Alliance building**: three states agree to treat an attack on one as an attack on all.

**(c) (i)** (1) **Confidence building**: telling the neighbour about exercises in advance so that they are not mistaken for an attack. (2) **Arms control**: seeking a regional cap on missile launchers, which limits weapons without abolishing them.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) An **arms race** is very costly and would take money from development. (2) Matching every weapon could make the neighbour feel threatened and **raise tension**, while a smaller, sufficient force still deters.

questions.passage_md:
**From the defence review of the imagined Republic of Veloria**

Our neighbour has doubled its missile force in five years. We will not match it weapon for weapon, but we will keep enough strength to make any attack too costly to try. We have also agreed with two nearby states that an attack on one will be treated as an attack on all three. At the same time, our officers will continue to tell our neighbour in advance about every large exercise near the border, and we will press for a regional agreement to cap the number of missile launchers.

children.stem_md: Which line shows Veloria relying on deterrence?
children.solution_md: Deterrence = preventing attack by raising its cost.

answer.model_answer_md: "We will keep **enough strength to make any attack too costly** to try."

children.stem_md: Name the component of traditional security shown by the agreement with two nearby states.
children.solution_md: A mutual-defence pact is an alliance.

answer.model_answer_md: **Alliance building**: three states agree to treat an attack on one as an attack on all.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Identify two forms of cooperation within traditional security that appear in the last sentence, and explain each.
children.solution_md: Advance notice = confidence building; a cap = arms control.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Confidence building**: telling the neighbour about exercises in advance so that they are not mistaken for an attack. (2) **Arms control**: seeking a regional cap on missile launchers, which limits weapons without abolishing them.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Why does Veloria choose not to "match it weapon for weapon"? Suggest two reasons.
alternatives.solution_md: Any two sensible reasons linked to cost or stability.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) An **arms race** is very costly and would take money from development. (2) Matching every weapon could make the neighbour feel threatened and **raise tension**, while a smaller, sufficient force still deters.

questions.stem_md: Read the source from a relief worker's diary in the imagined border town of Kesmara and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Crossing a border decides the term.

**(b)** The fever and feared outbreak point to epidemics.

**(c) (i)** One effect on migrants, one on hosts.

**OR (c) (ii)** Name human security and link it to protecting people from want and disease.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** People from **across the river** fleeing fighting are **refugees**; the flood-hit people from the **hill district** of the same country are **internally displaced persons**.

**(b)** A **health epidemic**: children are falling ill and an **outbreak** is feared, with very few doctors.

**(c) (i)** Migrants face **illness, hunger and lack of doctors** after long journeys. The host town faces **higher prices and pressure on services**, and some residents want the camp moved, so tension grows on both sides.

**OR (c) (ii)** **Human security** (in its broad sense): the camp protects **individuals** from hunger, disease and the effects of war and floods, rather than protecting a state's territory.

questions.passage_md:
**Diary of a relief worker, Kesmara camp (imagined)**

Monday. Two thousand more people arrived today from across the river, after fighting reached their villages. Many walked for four days. Another group came from inside this country, from the hill district where floods washed away their homes. We have one doctor for every five thousand people. Children are falling ill with fever and we fear an outbreak. The local market has doubled its prices and some townspeople say the camp should be moved. A team from an international medical charity is expected on Thursday with vaccines.

children.stem_md: Who among the new arrivals are refugees, and who are internally displaced persons?
children.solution_md: Crossing a border decides the term.

answer.model_answer_md: People from **across the river** fleeing fighting are **refugees**; the flood-hit people from the **hill district** of the same country are **internally displaced persons**.

children.stem_md: Identify one other new source of threat, besides migration, that appears in the diary.
children.solution_md: The fever and feared outbreak point to epidemics.

answer.model_answer_md: A **health epidemic**: children are falling ill and an **outbreak** is feared, with very few doctors.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): How does the diary show that migration can create insecurity for both migrants and the host community?
children.solution_md: One effect on migrants, one on hosts.

answer.model_answer_md: Migrants face **illness, hunger and lack of doctors** after long journeys. The host town faces **higher prices and pressure on services**, and some residents want the camp moved, so tension grows on both sides.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Which idea of security, traditional or human, best explains the work of the relief camp? Give a reason.
alternatives.solution_md: Name human security and link it to protecting people from want and disease.

answer.model_answer_md: **Human security** (in its broad sense): the camp protects **individuals** from hunger, disease and the effects of war and floods, rather than protecting a state's territory.

questions.stem_md: Read the source from the imagined white paper of Dravidia and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The focus is on people's well-being, not only borders.

**(b)** Working through the UN for rules = norms and institutions.

**(c) (i)** Map each pillar to a component.

**OR (c) (ii)** Agreement (or qualified agreement) with two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Human security** (non-traditional security): the security of **individual citizens** from want and disease.

**(b)** **Active work in the United Nations for fair rules** on disarmament and trade.

**(c) (i)** They correspond closely: (1) a deterrent army = **strengthening military capability**; (2) UN work = **international norms and institutions**; (3) dialogue at home = **meeting internal challenges democratically**; (4) growth for the poorest = **developing the economy** to remove poverty.

**OR (c) (ii)** Yes, largely. (1) Many threats such as **epidemics, drought and poverty** harm people without any army crossing a border. (2) A country whose citizens are poor and excluded is open to **internal conflict**, so development and inclusion are part of security.

questions.passage_md:
**Extract from a national security white paper, imagined Republic of Dravidia**

Security is not only about our borders. A citizen who cannot afford medicine, or a family that loses its harvest to drought, is not secure. Our plan therefore rests on four pillars: an army strong enough to deter attack; active work in the United Nations for fair rules on disarmament and trade; patient dialogue with groups at home who feel left out; and steady growth that brings jobs and schools to the poorest districts.

children.stem_md: Which notion of security does the first two sentences reflect?
children.solution_md: The focus is on people's well-being, not only borders.

answer.model_answer_md: **Human security** (non-traditional security): the security of **individual citizens** from want and disease.

children.stem_md: Which pillar of Dravidia's plan matches "strengthening international norms and institutions"?
children.solution_md: Working through the UN for rules = norms and institutions.

answer.model_answer_md: **Active work in the United Nations for fair rules** on disarmament and trade.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Compare Dravidia's four pillars with the components of India's security strategy.
children.solution_md: Map each pillar to a component.

answer.model_answer_md: They correspond closely: (1) a deterrent army = **strengthening military capability**; (2) UN work = **international norms and institutions**; (3) dialogue at home = **meeting internal challenges democratically**; (4) growth for the poorest = **developing the economy** to remove poverty.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Do you agree that "security is not only about our borders"? Give two reasons.
alternatives.solution_md: Agreement (or qualified agreement) with two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Yes, largely. (1) Many threats such as **epidemics, drought and poverty** harm people without any army crossing a border. (2) A country whose citizens are poor and excluded is open to **internal conflict**, so development and inclusion are part of security.

questions.stem_md: Read the source from an imagined school debate in Pune and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Wars between powers and treaties are traditional concerns.

**(b)** Any two of terrorism, epidemics, global warming.

**(c) (i)** Contrast the security of states with that of people.

**OR (c) (ii)** Any view is acceptable if supported by a sound argument and example.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Traditional** security: wars between states and arms control.

**(b)** **Terrorism** (attacks on crowded places) and **health epidemics** (viruses spreading through airports); global warming is also mentioned.

**(c) (i)** The answer depends on the **referent** of security. For **states**, the risk of great-power war may be lower; for **individuals**, new threats such as terrorism and disease may have grown. So the traditional view and the human-security view can reach different answers.

**OR (c) (ii)** Speaker C is most convincing: **both** kinds of threat exist. For example, treaties have limited some weapons between powers, yet a fast-spreading virus can still disrupt the lives of millions, so security must be judged for states **and** people.

questions.stem_md: Read the source on the imagined Saurya Islands health accord and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Neighbouring governments in one region.

**(b)** Charities and companies are non-state actors.

**(c) (i)** Cross-border spread; need for joint action.

**OR (c) (ii)** Name the threat, the method and the actors.

**OR (c) (ii)** It deals with a **non-traditional threat** (an epidemic) through **joint action** rather than force, at a **regional** level, and brings in **non-state actors** (charities, companies) along with governments.

The five island governments agree to share data on any new infectious disease within 48 hours of detection. A regional laboratory will be funded jointly. children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Why do the governments say that "closing ports alone cannot stop a disease"?
